audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (strict OUT, out-code lexical; dominant IN; rule 10 010 0010... kept as the dominant pattern)
audit.reasoning: Source side is as good as it gets: the deciding work is the 617-pp Mouton reference grammar (1994), the whole stress section (pp. 53-56) is held as page images, and the deciding quotation is verbatim on p. 53. The risk is not the source but the register. The catalog carries Wardaman as fixed-strict (in_strict True, 'verified-clean' from the sweep, never owner-reviewed), and the strict set is defined as 'one exceptionless weight-blind pattern per word length; a stated exception removes it'. The same held pages state exceptions in Merlan's own words: p. 53 'it is clear that there are different stress patterns within particular word classes, which must be recognized as part of the phonological structure of roots... For nouns, we must distinguish at least two different stress patterns... Among three-syllable and some longer words there is also a second pattern of ante-penultimate stress'
audit.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK — confirmed independently. I re-read the page images (not just the scanned),, and the scanned of PA54. p.53 carries both record sentences verbatim ('The most general word-level pattern in Wardaman is that a major stress, characterizable in terms of greater loudness and generally higher pitch, falls on the penultimate syllable of the inflected word. sources.quote: p. 53: "The most general word-level pattern in Wardaman is that a major stress, characterizable in terms of greater loudness and generally higher pitch, falls on the penultimate syllable of the inflected word. There is a tendency for this to be so regardless of the morphological composition of the word."
